planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed in fall on well-drained soil for a winter annual cover; bitter vetch is one of the most drought-tolerant of the vetches and thrives on thin, low-fertility, alkaline ground where hairy vetch struggles.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed onto a firm seedbed in fall and lightly incorporate, since bitter vetch germinates best with good seed-to-soil contact but shallow placement. This ancient Mediterranean legume tolerates drought, poor soils, and low rainfall far better than hairy vetch or common vetch, making it a useful option for dryland rotations and marginal ground. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it builds soil fertility and adds organic matter when mowed or incorporated before pods mature; because the seed contains compounds that can be toxic to non-ruminant livestock in quantity, it is grown strictly as a green manure or plow-down crop rather than for grazing or forage in most home and market garden settings.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Fact Sheets

planting.note: Broadcast fine seed onto a well-prepared, moist seedbed in fall; ball clover behaves much like a small-leaved white clover but reseeds itself reliably in Gulf South pastures and garden borders alike.

directions: Scatter the tiny seed over a shallow, firmed bed in early fall and roll or rake lightly so the seed is barely covered, since ball clover germinates poorly if buried deep. It grows low and spreading through winter, produces small round white-to-pink flower heads in spring, and sets abundant hard seed that lets stands persist year after year without replanting in mild Southern winters. Like other clovers it fixes atmospheric nitrogen for the following crop and its early spring bloom is a strong nectar source for honeybees and native pollinators before most garden flowers open.
sources: Oklahoma State University Extension — Forage Legume Guides

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto bare ground between rows or under trees in fall; Zorro fescue is a fine, low-growing, self-reseeding annual grass favored as living mulch in orchards and vineyards where it competes strongly against weeds without needing repeated mowing.

directions: Broadcast the fine seed over a lightly cultivated surface in fall and press it in with a roller or light raking, since Zorro fescue needs only shallow coverage to establish before winter rains. It germinates quickly, forms a dense, low mat of narrow leaves through winter and early spring, and reseeds itself so effectively that a single fall planting can persist as a cover for several seasons in a row. Growers value it in row middles and under perennial crops because its dense, shallow root mat suppresses weed germination and reduces erosion and dust without competing heavily for water once it dries down and goes dormant in early summer.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Cover Crops for Vineyards and Orchards

common_name: AU Early Cover Hairy Vetch (Early-Flowering Southern Hairy Vetch)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover crop; AU Early Cover, an Auburn University-bred hairy vetch selection, flowers earlier than common hairy vetch, letting Deep South growers terminate and plant into it sooner ahead of a warm-season crop.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed in early fall onto a well-prepared bed, inoculating with the proper rhizobium if the field has not grown vetch recently. AU Early Cover was selected for earlier flowering than standard hairy vetch, which allows it to reach peak nitrogen-fixing biomass and be mowed or rolled down several weeks sooner than later-flowering vetch strains, an important advantage for growers on tight spring planting schedules in the Gulf South. Like other hairy vetches its scrambling vines climb over themselves and any companion cereal, forming a thick nitrogen-rich mulch that suppresses weeds and feeds the following crop as it breaks down.
sources: Auburn University Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed shallowly in fall; Frontier is a widely grown balansa clover selection valued for fast establishment, flooding tolerance, and heavy reseeding in no-till Southern row-crop rotations.

directions: Plant seed shallowly on a firm, well-drained-to-moist seedbed in fall, since Frontier balansa clover germinates and grows quickly in cool weather and can even tolerate brief periods of waterlogged soil better than most other clovers. Its fine stems and small leaves knit into a dense winter mat that outcompetes cool-season weeds, and its abundant hard seed production means a single planting will often reseed itself for several following years. As a legume it fixes nitrogen for the subsequent crop, and its profuse small white flowers in spring draw in bees and other pollinators before most vegetables have bloomed.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension

common_name: Barkant Turnip (Forage and Cover Crop Turnip)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed in late summer to early fall for a fast-growing brassica cover; Barkant is a purple-topped turnip selection bred for heavy leafy top growth along with a large white root that scavenges nitrogen deep in the soil profile.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a shallow, well-prepared bed in late summer or early fall and rake lightly to cover, since fine brassica seed needs only light coverage to germinate quickly. Barkant produces a vigorous leaf canopy that shades out fall weeds within weeks along with a large, tapered white root that punches through compacted soil layers and pulls up leached nitrogen and other nutrients from deep in the profile. Left to winterkill or terminated before regrowth in spring, the rapidly decomposing roots and tops leave channels that improve water infiltration and add organic matter for the following crop.
sources: University of Wisconsin Extension — Forage and Cover Crop Brassicas

common_name: 4010 Forage Pea (Spring Field Pea Cover Crop)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in late summer for a fall cover; 4010 is a widely grown, tall, leafy field pea bred for quick biomass rather than seed harvest, commonly paired with oats as a companion cover crop.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed at a fairly high rate as soon as the ground can be worked in early spring, since 4010 peas germinate well in cool, moist soil but are not as winter-hardy as Austrian winter pea. Growers commonly mix it with spring oats, which give the tall, weak-stemmed vines something to climb and lean on, producing a combined stand that suppresses weeds quickly and can be mowed or grazed for forage or turned under as green manure. As a legume it fixes a meaningful amount of nitrogen for a following crop, and its rapid, dense early growth makes it a popular short-window cover between a spring vegetable harvest and a summer planting.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Cover Crops

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto a firm, well-drained seedbed in fall; Dalkeith is a classic, early-maturing subterranean clover cultivar that buries its own seed pods at the soil surface, giving it strong self-reseeding persistence as a low-growing living mulch.

directions: Broadcast seed over a firm bed in early fall and rake lightly, since subterranean clover establishes best with good seed-to-soil contact and adequate fall moisture. Dalkeith forms a dense, low, spreading mat of clover that carpets the ground through winter and, true to its name, buries its own developing seed pods just under the soil surface after flowering, an unusual trait that lets it reseed itself reliably without needing to be harvested or replanted. Because it grows so low and dense it works well as a living mulch under fruit trees, brambles, and other perennials, suppressing weeds, fixing nitrogen, and tolerating light foot traffic and mowing far better than taller clovers.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Cover Crops for Orchards

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed in fall on well-drained soil; Yuchi is the original widely commercialized arrowleaf clover cultivar, prized for tall growth, late spring flowering, and strong reseeding in Gulf South pastures and cover-crop rotations.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a well-prepared, well-drained bed in early fall and lightly cover, since arrowleaf clover seedlings are slow to establish but grow rapidly once cool, moist weather arrives. Yuchi grows much taller than crimson or white clover, standing well above competing winter weeds, and continues flowering later into late spring than most other winter annual clovers, extending the nitrogen-fixing and pollinator-forage window. Its arrow-shaped leaves and dense stands make it a long-standing standard for Deep South winter cover cropping, and it reseeds itself readily on well-drained soils if allowed to flower and set seed before termination.
